paragraphs: A fifth class of provisions in favor of the federal authority consists of the following restrictions on the authority of the individual States:

1. "No State shall enter into any treaty, alliance, or confederation; grant letters of marque and reprisal; coin money; emit bills of credit; make any thing but gold and silver a legal tender in payment of debts; pass any bill of attainder, ex post facto law, or law impairing the obligation of contracts; or grant any title of nobility."

The prohibition against treaties, alliances, and confederations is already part of the existing Articles of the Union, and for reasons that need no explanation it is copied into the new Constitution. The prohibition of letters of marque is also part of the old system, but the new Constitution extends it somewhat. Under the old Articles, the States could grant letters of marque after a declaration of war. Under the new Constitution, these licenses must be obtained from the government of the United States, in time of war as well as before war is declared. This change is fully justified by the advantage of uniformity in everything that relates to foreign powers, and by the advantage of having immediate responsibility to the nation for every act for which the nation itself will be held responsible.

The right of coining money, which the new Constitution takes from the States, was left in their hands by the Confederation as a right concurrent with that of Congress, with one exception: Congress alone had the right to regulate the alloy and value of the coin. Here, too, the new provision improves on the old. As long as the alloy and value were fixed by the general authority, a right of coinage in the particular States could have no effect except to multiply expensive mints and to diversify the forms and weights of the pieces in circulation. That second problem defeats one of the purposes for which the power was originally given to the federal head. As for the first, to the extent that State mints might spare the inconvenience of sending gold and silver to a central mint for recoinage, the same end can be attained just as well by local mints established under the general authority.

The extension of the prohibition to bills of credit, that is, paper money, must please every citizen in proportion to his love of justice and his knowledge of the true sources of public prosperity. Since the peace, America has suffered losses from the pestilent effects of paper money: on the confidence that must exist between man and man, on the confidence that must exist in the public councils, on the industry and morals of the people, and on the character of republican government. These losses amount to an enormous debt against the States that took this unadvised measure, a debt that must long remain unpaid. Or rather, they amount to an accumulated guilt that can be expiated in no other way than by a voluntary sacrifice, on the altar of justice, of the power that has been the instrument of it. In addition to these persuasive considerations, it may be observed that the same reasons which show the necessity of denying the States the power of regulating coin prove with equal force that they ought not to be at liberty to substitute a paper medium in the place of coin. If every State had a right to regulate the value of its coin, there might be as many different currencies as there are States, and so the intercourse among them would be impeded. Retrospective alterations in its value might be made, and so the citizens of other States would be injured and animosities would be kindled among the States themselves. The subjects of foreign powers might suffer from the same cause, and so the Union would be discredited and embroiled by the indiscretion of a single member. Not one of these harms is any less likely to follow from a power in the States to emit paper money than from a power to coin gold or silver. The power to make anything but gold and silver a tender in payment of debts is withdrawn from the States on the same principle as the power of issuing a paper currency.

Bills of attainder, ex post facto laws, and laws impairing the obligation of contracts are contrary to the first principles of the social compact and to every principle of sound legislation. The first two are expressly prohibited by the declarations prefixed to some of the State constitutions, and all three are prohibited by the spirit and scope of these fundamental charters. Our own experience has taught us, nevertheless, that additional fences against these dangers ought not to be omitted. The Convention has therefore done very properly in adding this constitutional bulwark in favor of personal security and private rights. And I am much deceived if, in doing so, they have not consulted as faithfully the genuine feelings of their constituents as their undoubted interests. The sober people of America are weary of the fluctuating policy that has directed the public councils. They have seen with regret and indignation that sudden changes and legislative interferences, in cases affecting personal rights, become profitable schemes in the hands of enterprising and influential speculators, and snares to the more industrious and less informed part of the community. They have seen, too, that one legislative interference is only the first link of a long chain of repetitions, every later interference being naturally produced by the effects of the one before. They very rightly infer, therefore, that some thorough reform is needed, one that will banish speculation on public measures, inspire a general prudence and industry, and give a regular course to the business of society. The prohibition with respect to titles of nobility is copied from the Articles of Confederation and needs no comment.

2. "No State shall, without the consent of the Congress, lay any imposts or duties on imports or exports, except what may be absolutely necessary for executing its inspection laws, and the net produce of all duties and imposts laid by any State on imports or exports, shall be for the use of the treasury of the United States; and all such laws shall be subject to the revision and control of the Congress. No State shall, without the consent of Congress, lay any duty on tonnage, keep troops or ships of war in time of peace, enter into any agreement or compact with another State, or with a foreign power, or engage in war unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."

The restraint on the power of the States over imports and exports is supported by all the arguments that prove the necessity of placing the regulation of trade in the federal councils. It is therefore needless to say more on this head, except that the way the restraint is qualified seems well calculated at once to secure to the States a reasonable discretion in providing for the convenience of their imports and exports, and to give the United States a reasonable check against the abuse of that discretion. The remaining particulars of this clause fall within reasonings that are either so obvious or so fully developed already that they may be passed over without remark.
The sixth and last class consists of the various powers and provisions by which effectiveness is given to all the rest.

1. The first of these is the "power to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof."

Few parts of the Constitution have been attacked with more intemperance than this one, yet on a fair investigation no part can appear more completely invulnerable. Without the SUBSTANCE of this power, the whole Constitution would be a dead letter. Those who object to the article as a part of the Constitution can therefore only mean that the FORM of the provision is improper. But have they considered whether a better form could have been substituted?

There are four other possible methods the Constitution might have taken on this subject. It might have copied the second article of the existing Confederation, which would have prohibited the exercise of any power not EXPRESSLY delegated. It might have attempted a positive enumeration of the powers comprehended under the general terms "necessary and proper." It might have attempted a negative enumeration of them, by specifying the powers excepted from the general definition. Or it might have been altogether silent on the subject, leaving these necessary and proper powers to construction and inference.

Had the Convention taken the first method, adopting the second article of the Confederation, it is evident that the new Congress would be continually exposed, as their predecessors have been, to a choice between two alternatives. They could construe the term "EXPRESSLY" so rigorously as to disarm the government of all real authority whatever, or so loosely as to destroy altogether the force of the restriction. It would be easy to show, if it were necessary, that Congress has not been able, and cannot be able, to execute any important power delegated by the Articles of Confederation without resorting, more or less, to the doctrine of CONSTRUCTION or IMPLICATION. The powers delegated under the new system are more extensive, so the government that administers it would find itself still more distressed by the alternative of betraying the public interests by doing nothing, or of violating the Constitution by exercising powers that are indispensably necessary and proper but are not EXPRESSLY granted.

Had the Convention attempted a positive enumeration of the powers necessary and proper for carrying their other powers into effect, the attempt would have required a complete digest of the laws on every subject to which the Constitution relates. That digest would have had to be adapted not only to the existing state of things but to all the possible changes the future may produce. For in every new application of a general power, the PARTICULAR POWERS that are the means of attaining the OBJECT of the general power must always necessarily vary with that object, and must often properly be varied even while the object remains the same.

Had they attempted to enumerate the particular powers or means that are not necessary or proper for carrying the general powers into execution, the task would have been no less chimerical. It would also have been open to this further objection: every defect in the enumeration would have been equivalent to a positive grant of authority. To avoid this consequence, they might have attempted a partial enumeration of the exceptions and described the remainder by the general terms NOT NECESSARY OR PROPER. But then the enumeration would have covered only a few of the excepted powers. These would be the ones least likely to be assumed or tolerated, because the enumeration would naturally select those that are least necessary or proper. And the unnecessary and improper powers left in the remainder would be less forcibly excepted than if no partial enumeration had been made.

Had the Constitution been silent on this head, there can be no doubt that all the particular powers required as means of executing the general powers would have passed to the government by unavoidable implication. No axiom is more clearly established in law or in reason than this: wherever the end is required, the means are authorized; wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary for doing it is included. Had the Convention pursued this last method, therefore, every objection now urged against their plan would remain in all its plausibility. And there would be the real drawback of failing to remove a pretext which may be seized on at critical moments to call into question the essential powers of the Union.

Suppose it is asked what the consequence will be if Congress should misconstrue this part of the Constitution and exercise powers not warranted by its true meaning. I answer that the consequence will be the same as if they should misconstrue or enlarge any other power vested in them. It will be the same as if the general power had been reduced to particulars and any one of these were violated. In short, it will be the same as if the State legislatures should violate their respective constitutional authorities. In the first case, the success of the usurpation will depend on the executive and judiciary departments, which are to expound and give effect to the legislative acts. In the last resort, a remedy must be obtained from the people, who can annul the acts of the usurpers by electing more faithful representatives. The truth is that this ultimate redress can be relied on more against unconstitutional acts of the federal legislature than of the State legislatures, for this plain reason: every such act of the former will be an invasion of the rights of the latter, and the State legislatures will always be ready to mark the innovation, to sound the alarm to the people, and to use their local influence to bring about a change of federal representatives. There is no such intermediate body, between the State legislatures and the people, with an interest in watching the conduct of the former. Violations of the State constitutions are therefore more likely to go unnoticed and unredressed.

2. "This Constitution and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof, and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land, and the judges in every State shall be bound thereby, any thing in the constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

The indiscreet zeal of the opponents of the Constitution has led them into an attack on this part of it also, although without it the Constitution would clearly and radically be defective. To be fully aware of this, we need only suppose for a moment that the supremacy of the State constitutions had been left complete by a saving clause in their favor.

In the first place, these constitutions invest the State legislatures with absolute sovereignty in all cases not excepted by the existing Articles of Confederation. So all the authorities contained in the proposed Constitution, to the extent that they exceed those enumerated in the Confederation, would have been annulled, and the new Congress would have been reduced to the same impotent condition as its predecessors.

In the next place, the constitutions of some of the States do not even expressly and fully recognize the existing powers of the Confederacy. An express saving of the supremacy of the State constitutions would, in such States, have called into question every power contained in the proposed Constitution.

In the third place, the constitutions of the States differ much from each other. It might therefore happen that a treaty or national law, of great and equal importance to all the States, would conflict with some State constitutions and not with others. It would consequently be valid in some of the States while having no effect in others.

In short, the world would have seen, for the first time, a system of government founded on an inversion of the fundamental principles of all government. It would have seen the authority of the whole society everywhere subordinate to the authority of the parts. It would have seen a monster, in which the head was under the direction of the members.

3. "The Senators and Representatives, and the members of the several State legislatures, and all executive and judicial officers, both of the United States and the several States, shall be bound by oath or affirmation to support this Constitution."

It has been asked why it was thought necessary that the State officials should be bound to support the federal Constitution, and unnecessary to impose a like oath on the officers of the United States in favor of the State constitutions.

Several reasons might be given for the distinction. I content myself with one, which is obvious and conclusive. The members of the federal government will have no part in carrying the State constitutions into effect. The members and officers of the State governments, on the contrary, will have an essential part in giving effect to the federal Constitution. The election of the President and the Senate will depend, in all cases, on the legislatures of the individual States. The election of the House of Representatives will equally depend on the same authority in the first instance, and will probably forever be conducted by the officers, and according to the laws, of the States.

4. Among the provisions for giving effectiveness to the federal powers, we might add those which belong to the executive and judiciary departments. But as these are reserved for particular examination in another place, I pass them over here.

We have now reviewed in detail all the articles that make up the sum of power delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government, and we are brought to this undeniable conclusion: no part of the power is unnecessary or improper for accomplishing the necessary objects of the Union. The question whether this amount of power shall be granted therefore resolves itself into another question: whether a government equal to the needs of the Union shall be established, or, in other words, whether the Union itself shall be preserved.
